title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: the mouse, the snake, and the moon who laughed. Today, the nine nights again, and the many ways India keeps them.

Think of the people who have looked after you. A grandmother who was all softness. A coach who was all edges and wouldn't let you quit. A teacher who said almost nothing, and somehow taught you the most. The same care, in very different faces. Some weeks you needed the soft one; some weeks, the one who pushed. Last time, the Goddess came out of the gods' light in one blazing form. But many Hindus don't meet her in just one form across these nights. They meet her in nine, one a night, and they divide the nights by what each one is for.
screen: `THE SAME CARE, DIFFERENT FACES.` → `ONE BLAZING FORM, LAST TIME.` → `NINE FACES, ONE A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: You know the story: the gods lose, their power becomes the Goddess, and Durga defeats the buffalo demon. Now, the nights. Many people honor a different form of the Goddess each night: nine forms, called the Navadurga. The first is Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain. Later come Kushmanda, who in the tradition smiled the universe into being, and Kalaratri, the dark night, fierce and protective. The ninth is Siddhidatri, the giver of perfection. Others divide the nights in threes. Three for Durga, strength, to clear away what's wrong. Three for Lakshmi, abundance, to fill the space with good. Three for Saraswati, wisdom, to understand it. Then the regions. In Bengal, Durga Puja tells the story as a homecoming: Durga returns to her parents' house with her children for a few days, then leaves again, and people cry at the immersion. In Gujarat, the dance called garba circles a lamp for the Goddess. In the south, the rows of dolls are called golu. And the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the tenth of victory, carries two stories. For many, it's Durga's victory. For many others, especially in the north, it's the day Rama defeated Ravana: Dussehra, when Ravana's effigy burns. Nobody has to choose. The nights are long, the forms are many, and the dawn comes to all of them. Nine nights, then the dawn.
screen: `NINE FORMS OF THE GODDESS.` · `STRENGTH, ABUNDANCE, WISDOM.` · `A HOMECOMING IN BENGAL.` · `THE TENTH DAY HOLDS TWO VICTORIES.` · then, large: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Name one small thing you won't let win tonight, the way Durga clears the ground. Then breathe in and name one good thing you want more of, the way Lakshmi fills it, and one thing you'd like to understand better, the way Saraswati lights it. Three breaths each, then rest.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept in dance, in pavilions, in dolls, and in fire, and a tenth day of victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. Strength, abundance and wisdom, three nights each. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus keep Navaratri in many regional ways: garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja pavilions in Bengal, golu doll displays in the south, and Ramlila plays in the north ending on Dussehra, when effigies of Ravana are burned.

sources.ref: Navadurga (the nine forms; listed in later devotional texts such as the Devi Kavacha)
Navaratri regional observance (garba, Durga Puja, golu, Ramlila and Dussehra)

notes: Navadurga order (Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri, Siddhidatri), usually cited from the Devi Kavacha. Confirm; only four named in script.
Kushmanda 'smiled the universe into being': traditional explanation of the name; confirm.
Three-three-three division (Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati): a common practice, not universal. Confirm.
Durga Puja as homecoming to her parents (Himalaya and Menaka) with her children: Bengali tradition. Confirm.
Ravana effigies on Dussehra; Ramlila plays in north India. Confirm.
